2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). Set `overall_rating = "NOT APPLICABLE (design fits no listed tool)"`, explain clearly in `why_tool_chosen` and `overall_narrative_summary` rather than forcing an inappropriate checklist, and still fill the 7 `cross_tool_domains` honestly from the paper!

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Low / Partial item non-response: Single-wave cross-sectional interviews with 12 participants involved no longitudinal panel attrition, but subsector participation varied by self-selection (8 water supply, 6 wastewater, 8 stormwater) and 4 of 12 interviewees ranked fewer than the requested 5 or 10 policies (PDF Page 9, Section 3).
cross_tool_domains.confounding: High concern (uncontrolled qualitative design): No counterfactual comparator or causal adjustment is attempted; the authors acknowledge that policies operate in interdependent chains alongside environmental shocks, pricing, and informal norms, preventing isolation of any single law's effect on resilience (PDF Pages 8, 10-11, Sections 2 and 3.1).
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Weak to moderate: The study identifies concrete federal, state, and local instruments (e.g., 1972 Clean Water Act, NPDES permits, 2013 CSO/SSO Consent Decree, 2009 Seattle Stormwater Code, SPU Director's Rules), but groups binding statutes together with capital plans, programs, and historic land purchases without formal statutory citations, doctrinal verification, or enforcement data, and mislabels/misdates the federal Safe Drinking Water Act as the 'National Safe Water Act (1972)' (PDF Pages 10, 15, 18-19, Sections 3.1 and 4.2).
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: High concern: Policy importance for resilience is operationalized solely through interviewees' subjective rankings of researcher-curated policy lists—retaining incomplete rankings and tied placements in point sums without normalization—and single-pass thematic grouping of open-ended answers with no reported recording/transcription protocol or inter-coder reliability check (PDF Pages 9-10, Sections 3 and 3.1).
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Weak (perceptual only): Primary outcomes are water professionals' subjective perceptions of which policies enable resilience and perceived future challenges, rather than objective empirical measures of service continuity, CSO frequency, water quality compliance, or shock recovery (PDF Pages 7-9, 11-23, Sections 2, 3, and 4-6).
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Moderate concern / Can't tell: No study protocol, interview guide appendix, or full candidate policy list is published, and qualitative findings are compressed into theme counts and summary bullet tables without any verbatim participant quotations or discussion of dissenting views (PDF Pages 9-24, Sections 3-6).
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: High concern: Purposive selection of 12 unnamed 'water professionals familiar with water services and resilience in the Seattle area' with zero reporting of recruitment frame, institutional affiliations, role breakdown, inclusion/exclusion criteria, or refusal rates (PDF Pages 8, 11, Sections 3 and 3.1).

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was there a clear statement of the aims of the research?
domain_ratings.justification: The authors explicitly state their research objectives: identifying historical development steps and current policies that local water professionals view as important for building resilience in Seattle's water supply, wastewater, and stormwater services, examining future challenges and recommendations, and determining the governance levels where resilience is most effectively implemented.

A qualitative approach combining documentary policy review and semi-structured expert interviews is appropriate for exploring practitioner perceptions of institutional history, formal policies, informal norms ('mindsets and habits'), and future governance challenges.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the research design appropriate to address the aims of the research?
domain_ratings.justification: The single-city case study design pairing historical/policy document review with five-question semi-structured interviews (structured policy-ranking elicitation plus open-ended questions on challenges and suggestions) is justified by reference to Seattle's institutional history and prior water-services history studies (Katko et al. 2006; Juuti et al. 2009).

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the recruitment strategy appropriate to the aims of the research?
domain_ratings.justification: Although the authors state they selected twelve 'knowledgeable and diverse' local water professionals familiar with water services and resilience in Seattle, they provide no information on how participants were identified or approached, which utilities/agencies or non-governmental bodies they worked for, their professional roles, or whether any invited experts declined.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 8, 11 (Sections 3 and 3.1 Limitations of the research)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the data collected in a way that addressed the research issue?
domain_ratings.justification: The paper outlines the five interview questions, notes that interviewees received two written definitions of resilience, and reports subsector response counts (8 water supply, 6 wastewater, 8 stormwater) and response similarity across the 12 individual 2018 interviews; however, it omits interview mode/setting, duration, whether interviews were audio-recorded or transcribed, and complete baseline policy lists presented to respondents.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Has the relationship between researcher and participants been adequately considered?
domain_ratings.justification: Despite the first author spending a year as a visiting scholar in Seattle (noted only in the end-of-paper biography) and the researchers pre-curating the lists of 'most significant policies' for interviewees to rank, there is no reflexive discussion of researcher positionality, prior professional relationships with interviewees, or how researcher pre-selection framed interviewee choices beyond allowing additions.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Have ethical issues been taken into consideration?
domain_ratings.justification: The paper contains no mention of institutional ethics review/approval, informed consent procedures, or confidentiality and anonymization safeguards for the twelve interviewed professionals.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 8-11 (Section 3 Methods — absent throughout text)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the data analysis sufficiently rigorous?
domain_ratings.justification: While Figure 5 illustrates the general thematic grouping of open-ended responses into nine categories, the paper does not report who performed the coding, whether coding was verified by a second researcher, or any verbatim participant quotes to substantiate themes; furthermore, in the point-tallying of rankings, four respondents ranked fewer than five or ten items and one assigned multiple tied first/second/third ranks, yet all responses were pooled without explaining any weighting adjustment.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Is there a clear statement of findings?
domain_ratings.justification: Findings are clearly organized and discussed across historical development steps (Section 4.1), current policies (Section 4.2), future challenges (Section 5, Table 1), and actionable suggestions (Section 6, Table 2) for each of the three subsectors (water supply, wastewater, stormwater), explicitly linking formal policies and informal rules back to the research aims.

Narrative assessment: The study offers practical, practitioner-grounded insight into how multilevel formal policies (federal Clean Water Act/NPDES mandates, consent decrees, local stormwater codes, watershed land acquisition, and utility asset/system plans) interact with informal institutional habits in urban water governance. However, its evidentiary value for causal policy evaluation and broader transferability is constrained by the small, non-transparently sampled group of 12 interviewees (6-8 per subsector) and reliance on perceived importance rather than measured resilience outcomes.
domain_ratings.rating: Moderate contextual value for urban water governance; limited causal and external validity
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 24-26 (Sections 7 Discussion and 8 Conclusions and recommendations)

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: Inha and Hukka (2019) present a single-city qualitative case study of Seattle's water supply, wastewater, and stormwater services based on a narrative policy/literature review and individual semi-structured interviews with 12 local water professionals (with 6 to 8 respondents answering per subsector). Appraised with the CASP Qualitative Checklist (the structured rank-order tallying across 6-8 respondents per subsector functions as an interview elicitation aid rather than a standalone quantitative survey component warranting MMAT), the study clearly states its aims (Q1: Yes), adopts an appropriate qualitative case-study approach (Q2: Yes; Q3: Yes), and presents well-structured subsector findings (Q9: Yes). However, substantial methodological concerns arise from unreported recruitment and participant institutional composition (Q4: Can't tell), omitted interview recording/transcription and setting details (Q5: Can't tell), lack of researcher reflexivity despite researcher curation of the candidate policy lists (Q6: No), absent ethics/consent reporting (Q7: Can't tell), and opaque coding verification alongside unadjusted pooling of incomplete and tied rankings with zero verbatim participant quotes (Q8: Can't tell). Moreover, both legal exposure importance and service resilience are assessed purely via interviewee perceptions rather than objective empirical outcome data.
raw_response.overall_rating: High methodological concern (4 Yes, 1 No, 4 Can't tell on Q1-Q9)
raw_response.study_design_identified: Single-city qualitative case study combining documentary/policy review with semi-structured expert interviews (structured policy-ranking elicitation and thematic content categorization) among 12 local water professionals
raw_response.where_found_summary: PDF Pages 1-3 (Abstract, Section 1 Introduction, Section 1.1 Background), PDF Pages 7-8 (Section 2 Conceptual framework), PDF Pages 8-11 (Section 3 Methods, Fig. 5, Section 3.1 Limitations), PDF Pages 11-26 (Sections 4-8 Results, Challenges, Suggestions, Discussion, Conclusions, and Author Biographies).
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The study's primary empirical component consists of 12 individual semi-structured expert interviews contextualized by a narrative literature and policy review in a single municipal setting (Seattle). Although three of the five interview prompts asked respondents to rank policies from a researcher-curated list and tallied rank points (across n=6 to 8 respondents per subsector) alongside frequency counts of coded open-ended themes, there is no quantitative sampling frame, statistical estimation, or distinct quantitative study strand; thus CASP Qualitative Checklist is the appropriate primary qualitative case-study instrument rather than MMAT or ROBINS-I.
